title: The AI lead response playbook for car dealerships
summary: Implement dealership AI lead response with practical templates, ownership rules, escalation paths and pass/fail tests for booking, opt-outs and failed handoffs.
body_markdown:
An AI lead-response playbook should tell the store what to send, where a reply goes and how to test that the workflow works. A fast acknowledgement is only the first step. The customer needs an answer or an owned action.


Use this implementation asset alongside the[revenue capture hub](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/pillars/dealership-revenue-capture) . For timing definitions and reporting, use the separate[lead-response-time guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/dealership-lead-response-time) ; for stages and overdue work, use the[lead-management guide](https://www.useclearline.com/blog/why-dealerships-lose-leads) .


## Prepare the facts and routing rules


Before enabling replies, define the authoritative inventory source, dealership hours, calendars, supported booking types, staff directory, approved offers and escalation owners. A missing feed or unclear policy should produce a request for staff help, not an invented answer.


Decide which channels the customer may be contacted on and apply the store’s contact limits, consent and opt-out process. The examples below are templates for review, not messages ready to send to every customer. Substitute accurate details and the required channel-specific opt-out wording before use.


## Three first-response templates


### Vehicle inquiry


> Hi \[first name\], this is \[name\] from \[dealership\]. I saw your question about \[vehicle or stock number\]. \[Answer using the verified inventory record, or say staff will confirm it.\] Would you like help with that vehicle or a time to visit?


Use the customer’s actual question. If availability is unconfirmed, do not say the unit is available. Final price, payments, trade values and incentives require the store’s approved source or authorized employee.


### Appointment request


> Hi \[first name\], this is \[name\] from \[dealership\]. You asked about \[test drive or service\]. \[Offer verified times from an enabled calendar, or explain that the booking team will confirm a time.\] Which option works for you?


An offered time is not a confirmed appointment. Complete the approved booking action, inspect its result and send the details only after confirmation.


### Request for a person or a policy exception


> Hi \[first name\], this is \[name\] from \[dealership\]. I’ll ask \[responsible person or department\] to help with \[specific question\]. \[State a callback time only if the team has committed to it.\] Is \[verified contact method\] the best way to reach you?


Create owned work for the receiving team. Do not end with “someone will call” unless the workflow makes that promise actionable.


## Route the reply by the work it creates


Customer reply Required action Human owner


Vehicle availability question Use the approved feed or request verification; preserve the stock number Sales / inventory contact


Test-drive or service booking Use an enabled calendar and allowed appointment type; verify the result Booking owner for that department


Final price, payment, trade value or approval Escalate without making an unsupported commitment Authorized sales / finance employee


Complaint, safety concern or complex service question Route with the customer’s context Manager / service advisor


Request for a person Transfer or create a callback task with a fallback Named receiving employee / department


Opt-out or wrong recipient Apply the channel contact rule, record the request and stop the affected outreach Campaign owner for exception review


Reply after assignment changes Deliver to the current owner and prevent parallel outreach Current opportunity owner


Put the table in the operating instructions and assign real names or department queues. Configure only the actions your product supports. If a rule requires a manual task or review, make that step explicit.


## Define what stops or changes a sequence


Specify behavior when the customer books, replies, requests a person, opts out, purchases, enters another active workflow or is identified as the wrong recipient. Test whether the stop applies to the relevant sequence, channel or broader store policy.


Do not let a delayed automated message continue a conversation an employee has already taken over. If another CRM runs outreach, document which system owns the cadence and how the other learns about the change.


## Acceptance tests before launch


Use test records and record pass/fail, the responsible person and the fix for each failure.


Test Pass condition


Available vehicle Reply uses the actual stock record and current approved facts


Sold or unavailable vehicle No false availability; alternative or staff action stays within approved rules


Payment question No invented payment or approval; request reaches an authorized employee


No valid appointment slot No false booking; customer receives an owned next step


Book, reschedule and cancel Only permitted actions run; correct calendar and resulting record are verified


Employee unavailable Failed transfer or callback request reaches the fallback owner


Customer corrects a detail Updated information is used in the next reply and staff can find it


Opt-out / wrong number Affected outreach stops and the request is visible for review


Duplicate lead / concurrent campaign The store avoids conflicting outreach under its defined ownership rule


Failed integration action No success confirmation; unresolved work has an owner and retry/recovery path


Some tests may require a staff step. Passing means the whole workflow completes under its defined rule, not that every step is automated.


## Keep an escalation sheet next to the workflow


For each exception, record the trigger, receiving person/department, hours, fallback, required context and completion evidence. Review unanswered handoffs and failed actions at the start and end of each shift.


Change the template or routing rule when a review finds the same failure repeatedly. Keep a dated version so managers know which wording and workflow produced the result.


## Configure and verify our workflows


We support[inbound conversations](https://www.useclearline.com/product/inbound) ,[campaigns](https://www.useclearline.com/product/campaigns) and a native[CRM workspace](https://www.useclearline.com/product/crm) . You can enable booking, cancellation, rescheduling, inventory search and PBS-dependent repair-order status separately. Booking jobs require selected calendars.


Review your supported cadence, channel and stop-condition controls in a[campaign demonstration](https://www.useclearline.com/demo) . Show the customer record, opportunity and next task, then inspect exactly which action occurred. Do not infer universal automatic stage or task updates from the presence of a conversation summary.


[Book a workflow demonstration](https://www.useclearline.com/demo) with a vehicle question, a booking request and a failed handoff. Use this acceptance table to evaluate the result.


## Frequently asked questions


What should an AI first response include? +


Identify the dealership, address the actual question using approved facts, and offer one useful next step. Use accurate customer details and the contact rules required for the channel.


Should AI quote prices, payments or incentives? +


Only within the store’s approved sources and permissions. Escalate unverified or exception-sensitive terms to an authorized employee.


What happens when an employee cannot accept a handoff? +


The playbook must define a fallback owner and actionable callback/task process. Test it before launch and review unresolved handoffs each shift.


How is this different from a response-time guide? +


This playbook defines templates, routing, stop conditions and acceptance tests. The response-time guide defines how to measure speed and interpret the result.
